comparison: Both evaluations support the methodological approach and control system design (C2, C26, C33-C36, C87-C95). OpenEval emphasizes the well-documented rationale and implementation details, while peer reviewers highlight the novelty, elegance, and lack of required surgical intervention. Both agree on the strength of the approach, though peer reviewers focus more on the no-calibration aspect (C7, C8) which OpenEval addresses separately in R2.

Both evaluations support the Exp1 results (C3-C5, C37-C44) showing high success rates and comparable movement times. However, peer reviewers raise concerns about the interpretation of movement time distributions, requesting individual participant data to verify that distributions (not just means) are similar to natural movements. OpenEval accepts the statistical results without this caveat.

Both evaluations support the generalization results from Exp2 (C47-C56), showing the Generic ANN performed nearly as well as Own ANN. OpenEval provides detailed statistical validation, while peer reviewers accept the results and express interest in the training methodology. Both acknowledge the moderate increase in compensatory movements as reasonable.

Both evaluations support the clinical application results from Exp3 (C57-C74, C116). OpenEval notes the small sample size as a limitation but finds the evidence strong. Peer reviewers acknowledge this as a strength, particularly the no-calibration aspect, though Reviewer 2 questions the interpretation of 'no training' versus 'no familiarization.' Both agree on the positive qualitative feedback.

OpenEval supports the real-world feasibility results (C6, C75-C86) while noting limited testing as a weakness. Peer reviewers are more uncertain, raising significant concerns about the teleoperation setup not being physically attached to users, the limited range of object distances, and the impact of device weight on shoulder movements. Both note the lower success rate compared to VR, but peer reviewers emphasize practical deployment challenges more strongly.

Both address limitations regarding movement goal input and real-world deployment (C96-C102). OpenEval views the acknowledgment of limitations as demonstrating scientific rigor and finds the discussion balanced. Peer reviewers are more uncertain, emphasizing these as significant concerns for practical deployment, particularly the reliance on precise target position knowledge and the non-trivial computer vision challenges. The editor concludes additional improvements are needed.

Both evaluations support the participant demographics and ethical compliance (C117-C124). OpenEval finds the sample sizes reasonable for proof-of-concept work, and peer reviewers explicitly note the work was tested with a reasonable number of subjects including those with limb loss. No concerns were raised by either evaluation.

Both evaluations support the detailed methodological specifications (C30, C32, C125-C134). OpenEval emphasizes the reproducibility enabled by clear documentation of ANN architecture, training parameters, and data quality control. Peer reviewers accept these methods without challenge, though express interest in understanding the relative importance of different input features.

Both evaluations support the discussion of hardware limitations requiring actuated wrist joints (C103-C106). OpenEval notes this as appropriately cited, and peer reviewers acknowledge it as a practical constraint rather than a research flaw. Both accept this as a reasonable limitation of current prosthetic hardware availability.

Both address future applications and complementary approaches (C107-C110 overlap). OpenEval finds the discussion of hand control scope and complementary approaches well-reasoned and appropriately cited. Peer reviewers accept these as reasonable future directions, with suggestions for expanding grasp command methods and noting potential for meaningful activities of daily living.

Both address phantom limb pain applications (C111-C115). OpenEval rates this as uncertain, noting it is speculative but plausible with supporting citations about mirror therapy limitations, but lacking validation data. Peer reviewers support this as a reasonable future direction without challenging the speculation, suggesting acceptance of the proposed application.

Partial overlap on movement time interpretation (C5, C40, C41). OpenEval supports the statistical results from Exp1. Peer R6 questions whether the ANN's instantaneous predictions might artificially reduce movement times, suggesting the approach demonstrates feasibility but requires additional improvements. This represents a more critical interpretation of the same data.

Partial overlap on methodological approach (C27-C29, C31, C89). OpenEval R1 emphasizes the well-documented implementation details and rationale. Peer R8 accepts the workspace spanning methodology without challenge, though notes concerns about unconstrained reaches making additional activities problematic. Both support the approach but with different emphases.

OpenEval R6 supports the problem context and motivation claims (C1, C14-C23), noting accurate citation of prior work and solid motivation. No corresponding peer review evaluation specifically addresses these background and motivation claims.

OpenEval R7 supports the characterization of prior work and its limitations (C24-C25). While peer R1 includes C24 in its claim set, it does not specifically evaluate these claims about the authors' prior work. OpenEval finds this appropriately sets up the current improvements.

OpenEval R13 supports background claims about established techniques (C11-C13), noting accurate citations providing relevant context. No corresponding peer review evaluation addresses these background claims.

Peer R6 questions movement time interpretation across multiple experiments (C5, C32, C40, C41, C50, C51, C62, C63, C84-C86), suggesting the ANN's instantaneous predictions might artificially reduce times and requesting distribution data. While OpenEval addresses these claims in R2, R3, R4, and R5, it does not consolidate this cross-cutting concern about movement time interpretation methodology.

Peer R8 supports the workspace spanning methodology (C27-C31, C89) without challenge, though notes the unconstrained nature of reaches could complicate restoring additional activities. OpenEval addresses these claims partially in R1 and R8 but does not create a dedicated evaluation for this specific methodological aspect.
